115	
116	## Guidance
117	
118	When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
119	must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
120	`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
121	smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
122	in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
123	such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
124	are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

127	# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals
128	
129	## Guidance
130	
131	For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
132	artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
133	unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.
134	
135	Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
136	explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
137	unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
138	of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.
139	
140	Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
141	installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
142	availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
143	execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
144	terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.
145	
146	When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
147	replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
148	unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
149	complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.
150	
151	Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
152	discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
153	because completing it is necessary to proceed.
154	
155	Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
156	workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
157	must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
158	only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
159	earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
160	authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
161	states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
162	unrun.
163	
164	---
165	# Target Audience
166	
167	## Guidance
168	
169	Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
170	intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
171	project's vocabulary.
172	
173	Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
174	that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
175	repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
176	vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
177	“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
178	feature.”
179	
180	Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
181	label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
182	decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
183	actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
184	dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.
185	
186	Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
187	artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
188	state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
189	assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
190	relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
191	workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.
192	
193	When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
194	observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
195	it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
196	inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
197	reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
198	obtain the missing evidence.
199	
200	When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
201	"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
202	behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
203	value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
204	because it lies between two observations.
205	
206	For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
207	commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
208	not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
209	the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.
210	
211	Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.
212	
213	Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
214	labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
215	action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
216	identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
217	Rewrite it when the answer is no.
218	
219	---
220	# User Request Scheduling
221	
222	## Guidance
223	
224	When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
225	versus Terminal Goals rule.
226	
227	When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
228	immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
229	that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
230	the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
231	first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.
232	
233	When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
234	when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
235	capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
236	budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

# File Links

## Guidance

When a reader-visible response refers to a local file, use a Markdown link: `[Description](target)`. The description
must contain the target's filename and, when available, append a colon followed by its decimal line number, such as
`ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7`. When the response refers to different targets with the same filename, include the
smallest subset of each target's full path that lets the reader distinguish them; otherwise do not include a directory
in the description. The target may use the full available path. Before finalizing, reject a bracketed local-file label
such as `[ReceiptDownloadEndpoint.java:7]` unless it has the Markdown link target required by this rule; brackets alone
are not a link. Write the target immediately after `(` and before `)`, without leading or trailing whitespace.

---
# Intermediate versus Terminal Goals

## Guidance

For every workflow, name the terminal goal and the acceptance evidence that proves it. Classify plans, staging
artifacts, repairs, migrations, investigations, commits, recorded transitions, and verification as intermediate tasks
unless their evidence proves every terminal acceptance condition.

Record every required terminal gate and its required evidence before execution. Mark each gate passed, failed, unrun, or
explicitly excluded by the user; do not infer a passed state from a related check. A failed or unrun required gate is an
unmet terminal condition. A clean build, an inspected result, a repaired intermediate artifact, or an existing sequence
of commits cannot substitute for the gate that the workflow requires.

Match evidence to the claim each terminal gate makes. Evidence that establishes only an enabling condition—such as
installation, configuration, authorization, discovery, connection, initialization, or process start—may pass only an
availability gate. It cannot pass a behavior or outcome gate. For those gates, require evidence from the relevant
execution boundary that the required behavior ran and produced its required effect. When availability itself is the
terminal outcome, record availability as that gate's claim.

When new work arises, classify it before acting. It supports the current terminal goal unless the user explicitly
replaces or expands that goal. Record its own completion evidence separately. After it completes, re-evaluate the
unchanged terminal conditions and continue from the next unmet condition. Do not report completion, return control as
complete, or discard required follow-up work on intermediate evidence.

Treat a user instruction as a goal change only when it explicitly replaces or expands the requested terminal outcome. A
discovered prerequisite, failure, repair, workaround, or implementation detail does not change that outcome merely
because completing it is necessary to proceed.

Before an irreversible action that represents completion—such as committing, finalizing, publishing, or declaring a
workflow complete—record the user-authorized scope and compare it with terminal acceptance evidence. Every scoped item
must have completion evidence or an explicit user-authorized exclusion. A prior result may reduce the remaining scope
only when durable evidence proves it covered the same item under the same governing contract; a tidy-looking history, an
earlier status claim, or partial inspection is intermediate evidence, not proof. Otherwise continue across the full
authorized scope. Immediately before the terminal action or claim, repeat that comparison, including the recorded gate
states, and report remaining work instead of success when any item is unaccounted for or any required gate is failed or
unrun.

---
# Target Audience

## Guidance

Write every user response, prompt or rule file, source comment or Javadoc, command help text, and error message so its
intended reader can identify the relevant actor, input or state, action, result, and next decision without knowing this
project's vocabulary.

Prefer common precise language. Introduce a specialized or abstract workflow term only when it conveys a distinction
that common language loses; define it at its first reader-visible use in concrete terms. Do not define a term by
repeating it or replacing it with other undefined project terms. When a plain definition still needs workflow
vocabulary, add the shortest before-to-after example that shows the ordinary observable effect. For example, replace
“whole later correction commit” with “a later commit containing only changes that complete or correct one earlier
feature.”

Apply the same test to a new category, exception, boundary, or conclusion. It is unexplained when a reader must accept a
label such as “family”, “complete”, or “required” without being told which observable facts make it true and what
decision those facts require. Do not let an example or desired result define that boundary. At its first use, name the
actor, observable facts, acceptance evidence, and resulting decision; then check one meaningful analogous case and one
dissimilar case to ensure the wording states the shared condition rather than the example's label.

Do not use an internal state or compound relationship label as its own explanation in reader-facing prose. Name the
artifact or action it represents and why it matters. When the label conceals why an operation cannot work in a receiving
state, explain the smallest causal sequence before proposing a remedy: the original and receiving states, operation,
assumption missing from the receiving state, and observable result. Then create a version of the selected operation that
relies only on the receiving state and verify its intended result. When the workflow lacks that capability, say that the
workflow and tool need a feature to create and verify it; do not imply that the change is impossible.

When warning that a check, observation, or result cannot establish a conclusion, explain the failed reasoning as an
observable sequence. Name the check or observation, the conclusion it might lead the reader to draw, the inputs or cases
it leaves unexamined, and the resulting incorrect decision. Then state the replacement procedure: which artifacts or
inputs to examine, the comparison or decision to make, and the evidence that completes it. Do not say only that the
reader must not rely on, assume, or treat something as proof; that does not explain why it is insufficient or how to
obtain the missing evidence.

When explaining a diagnosis, do not replace observed evidence and its limited conclusion with an internal label such as
"the model-facing boundary." First name the producer, the artifact, the differing observed values, and the resulting
behavior in their causal order. Then state only what those observations establish. If the unobserved step that changes a
value is not yet known, say that it remains to be located and name the next check; do not assign it to a component merely
because it lies between two observations.

For example, a patch prepared after `addsValidation()` exists can rely on that unchanged nearby text. When an earlier
commit lacks the method, Git cannot locate the patch. Create a version relative to that earlier commit and verify it. Do
not lead with labels such as “source tree,” “destination tree,” “target-adapted,” “reconstruction,” or “context” unless
the reader has first been given this explanation or the term is immediately defined in it.

Do not explain ordinary, broadly understood technical terms unless the project gives them a specialized meaning.

Before finalizing prose, review the actual draft—not only these guidelines—for internal labels, compound relationship
labels, and unexplained workflow terms. For each one, either replace it with the concrete artifact, relationship, and
action it hides, or define it where it first appears. Then ask whether the intended reader can paraphrase the sentence,
identify the required action or decision, and explain any necessary specialized term without reading another artifact.
Rewrite it when the answer is no.

---
# User Request Scheduling

## Guidance

When a user request arrives during active work, acknowledge receiving it immediately. Classify it using the Intermediate
versus Terminal Goals rule.

When the request relates to the current terminal goal, treat it as steering for the current work and apply it
immediately. An explicit request to stop, cancel, replace, or do work instead of the current goal is related steering
that changes the terminal goal; apply it immediately and retain or discard queued goals only as the user directs. When
the request is unrelated, append it to the queued goals after every request already queued; process queued goals
first-come-first-served after the current terminal goal completes.

When translating a user request into a tool or workflow invocation, supply an optional limit, policy, or setting only
when the user explicitly provides it or the request identifies the project's documented default. Authorization to use a
capability does not authorize selecting its optional parameters. For example, create or resume a goal without a token
budget unless the user states one; pass a stated budget exactly.

# Safe Work Delegation

## Design Goals

- Allocate workflow work to the least costly authority that can verify or decide it: deterministic work to authoritative
  automation, bounded review to independently checkable delegation, and high-judgment decisions to the authority able to
  evaluate them.

## Guidance

When designing, updating, or executing a prompt-driven workflow, first classify every operation as deterministic,
bounded-review, or high-judgment work.

Move deterministic operations into authoritative automation, normally a CLI. The automation owns authoritative-state
capture, derived paths and arguments, validation, generated artifacts, recovery evidence, execution, and
machine-readable diagnostics. Do not leave an agent or human to reproduce those operations.

Delegate bounded-review work to a cheaper model only when its acceptance check is materially cheaper, narrower, or more
reliable than independently performing the delegated work. Give it explicit inputs, a bounded deliverable, and
acceptance evidence. Treat its result as a candidate until the specified deterministic check or higher-authority review
accepts it.

When a delegated response must use a specific form, state that form in the task sent to the recipient. Name the
recipient's injected response contract and required form when one exists; otherwise specify every required response
component. Do not rely on a parent-only requirement or generic handoff language.

Keep high-judgment work with the higher-level model: semantic design, intent, topic boundaries, earliest complete
placement, conflict resolution, security-sensitive decisions, and any result whose verification would require redoing
the same analysis. Do not delegate merely to create an appearance of independent review.

When a cheaper agent is available and delegation satisfies these conditions, use it; otherwise continue directly.

1	
2	## Design Goals
3	
4	- Test observable behavior with isolated, controlled inputs and state, ensuring each claim, exercised boundary, and
5	  assertion describe that same outcome and remain distinct from structural artifact validation.
6	- Ensure an artifact-wide audit finds every executable verification artifact whose claimed outcome is not directly
7	  exercised and observed.
8	- Make application behavior directly and safely testable in the same process by passing environmental dependencies
9	  explicitly when shared process state would otherwise prevent isolation.
10	- Verify meaningful changes efficiently with the narrowest relevant test and the complete suite before handoff.
11	
12	## Guidance
13	
14	Test observable behavior with controlled inputs rather than machine-specific configuration or implementation details.
15	Each test owns its fixtures and mutable state. Avoid tests that primarily validate third-party tools; test the
16	application's interpretation, command construction, error handling, and integration behavior instead.
17	
18	Choose the test language from the behavior being claimed, not from the fact that it uses a command, files, or another
19	tool. Test behavior in the same process when its dependencies can be injected. Use the project's shell-test framework
20	when the claimed behavior depends on POSIX-shell parsing, expansion, exit handling, or a packaged shell-facing
21	interface. Do not use a shell test merely because application code invokes another command; do not use a facade that
22	skips shell behavior a shell contract must prove.
23	
24	Do not fork a process merely to isolate the current directory, environment variables, standard streams, clocks, random
25	sources, or other shared process state. Refactor the owned behavior to accept that dependency explicitly, and have the
26	existing production entry point obtain the real value and delegate to the new operation. Tests must invoke that
27	operation with an isolated value they own, such as a temporary directory for the current directory. This preserves
28	production behavior while making parallel tests deterministic and self-contained.
29	
30	Apply the temporary-resource ownership convention to every fixture a test creates. A test must clean up its fixture even
31	when setup, an assertion, or the behavior under test fails.
32	
33	Do not rerun an unchanged test command merely for reassurance. Run the narrowest relevant test after a meaningful
34	change, then the complete verification suite before handoff.
35	
36	Before accepting any test, state in one plain sentence what it says happens and identify the operation that makes it
37	happen. For example: "Installing the extension makes the host run its startup hook." If the test does not run the
38	operation that makes its claimed behavior happen, rename it as a structure test or move it to the supported consumer
39	entry point.
40	
41	Derive each test from the observable claim it makes. A test must run the part of the system it says it tests: its name,
42	documented claim, controlled input, exercised boundary, and assertion must all describe the same observable outcome. Any
43	test that claims an externally observable outcome must run the boundary that produces it and assert the result.
44	Consumer, integration, lifecycle, installation, registration, and execution claims are non-exhaustive examples. Do not
45	prove such a claim by reading source files, generated configuration text, or asserting literal fragments.
46	
47	When auditing executable verification artifacts across an existing scope, enumerate every test, scenario,
48	fixture-backed check, and executable example. For each one, apply the claim, exercised-boundary, and
49	observable-assertion requirements in this rule. Correct every unsupported claim by narrowing it, adding the missing
50	direct exercise and assertion, or splitting independently observable outcomes.
51	
52	Structural artifact tests are allowed when their claim is limited to packaged layout or validity. Build or obtain the
53	assembled artifact, parse its structured metadata, and assert required files, references, and formats using the artifact
54	as the input. Name these tests as packaging, structure, or validation tests, not as runtime registration or execution
55	tests. Keep structural coverage separate from behavior coverage; neither substitutes for the other.
56	
57	Use the complete artifact produced by the production packaging operation. Do not extract one resource and add a fake
58	launcher, script, or other missing component before calling it an assembled artifact. A test that supplies such a
59	fixture may claim only the behavior of the component that consumes it; it may not claim packaging, registration,
60	installation, lifecycle, or execution behavior. A manifest, hook, or configuration file is a valid structural input only
61	when its exact format is the documented external artifact contract being validated.

Do not rerun an unchanged test command merely for reassurance. Run the narrowest relevant test after a meaningful
change, then the complete verification suite before handoff.

Before accepting any test, state in one plain sentence what it says happens and identify the operation that makes it
happen. For example: "Installing the extension makes the host run its startup hook." If the test does not run the
operation that makes its claimed behavior happen, rename it as a structure test or move it to the supported consumer
entry point.

Derive each test from the observable claim it makes. A test must run the part of the system it says it tests: its name,
documented claim, controlled input, exercised boundary, and assertion must all describe the same observable outcome. Any
test that claims an externally observable outcome must run the boundary that produces it and assert the result.
Consumer, integration, lifecycle, installation, registration, and execution claims are non-exhaustive examples. Do not
prove such a claim by reading source files, generated configuration text, or asserting literal fragments.

When auditing executable verification artifacts across an existing scope, enumerate every test, scenario,
fixture-backed check, and executable example. For each one, apply the claim, exercised-boundary, and
observable-assertion requirements in this rule. Correct every unsupported claim by narrowing it, adding the missing
direct exercise and assertion, or splitting independently observable outcomes.

Structural artifact tests are allowed when their claim is limited to packaged layout or validity. Build or obtain the
assembled artifact, parse its structured metadata, and assert required files, references, and formats using the artifact
as the input. Name these tests as packaging, structure, or validation tests, not as runtime registration or execution
tests. Keep structural coverage separate from behavior coverage; neither substitutes for the other.

Use the complete artifact produced by the production packaging operation. Do not extract one resource and add a fake
launcher, script, or other missing component before calling it an assembled artifact. A test that supplies such a
fixture may claim only the behavior of the component that consumes it; it may not claim packaging, registration,
installation, lifecycle, or execution behavior. A manifest, hook, or configuration file is a valid structural input only
when its exact format is the documented external artifact contract being validated.

1	# Declared change: downloadable order receipts
2	
3	Add a customer receipt-download endpoint before the Friday release. It must let a signed-in customer download only that
4	customer's receipt. The release must be deployable without manual secret changes, preserve the project's third-party
5	notice obligations, remain responsive for large receipts, explain a denied download in plain language, and have
6	automated verification of the authorization and download behavior.

4

summary:
## Findings

- **[CHANGE.md:6](/home/gili/cat/worktrees/v1.0/docs/changelog/1.0/captures/reviews/languages/java/runs/claude-cat-testing/claude/msp6udut-b61ke6bu4w/project/.claude/worktrees/agent-a8168ceb3751fdfde/CHANGE.md#L6) Required authorization and download verification is absent**
  - **Evidence:** The declared change requires automated verification of authorization and download behavior, but the fixture contains no test files or test commands; the endpoint implementation is the only Java source.
  - **Consequence:** There is no executable evidence that an authenticated owner can download their receipt, that another customer is denied, or that the response contains the intended receipt data, so the required behavior cannot be established or protected from regression.
  - **Correction:** Add automated endpoint-level tests covering a signed-in receipt owner’s successful download and a different signed-in customer’s denied request, with assertions on the returned/downloaded content and denial response.
